description:
List events between min_time and max_time. action_ids are what was
done at each event, the first setting its color (action_names gives
their names). effective_priority is the priority that applies:
the event's own priority, falling back to the highest priority of its
actions and goals.
recurring_event_id is the id of an instance's recurring
series (see get_recurrence and update_recurrence to read and edit the
series as a whole); event_label_id is the calendar label derived from
its first action. facts are what compaction established about a past
event: where, who with, who for, and a note on each person there (see
PublicEvent). action_names, effective_priority,
recurring_event_id and event_label_id are read-only: update_event and
create_event ignore them. repeat is write-only, and never listed.

`person_id`: only the events whose facts name that person (with, for,
or noted) -- or a plain circle they're in now, without them in its
except -- an id, or a name get_person takes; or a community's id, for
the events naming it. Quick over any span,
years included: search a person's history with a wide range.

is_cancelled is read-only: update_event refuses to set it -- cancel
an event with delete_event, which says whether the cancellation counts
against follow-through.

action_ids are what was done at the event (see get_actions), the
first setting its label and color; setting them is how an event is
tied to actions. Each is an action's id, taking an even part of the
remaining time (what the minutes and percents leave), or an object
{action_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?}: minutes (a fixed share),
percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining true for its part of
the remaining time as well. The minutes must fit in the event and the
percents add up to no more than 100; read back, minutes are cut to fit
an event shortened since. action_names (their names, in the same order) and
event_label_id (derived from the first action) are read-only: an
update ignores them.

actions_from_label is true when an event was never given actions, so
its action_ids are inferred from its label (the action that holds the
label), not stored. Sending it back with actions_from_label still true
leaves them inferred, whatever action_ids says; to store actions, send
action_ids with actions_from_label false (or left out).

effective_priority is read-only: the priority that applies, i.e.
priority falling back,
when the event doesn't set one, to the highest (lowest-numbered)
priority among its actions (each action's own, or its nearest
group's) and its goals (each goal's own, or its nearest parent's, or
else 3). Kept separate from priority so that sending a listed event
straight back to update_event never copies that priority onto the
event itself, which would stop it following later changes to its
actions and goals. An update ignores it.

recurring_event_id is read-only too, and an update ignores it as
well: it's assigned by Google and can't be set at all.

goals are the goals the event is for (see get_goals): each a goal_id,
with minutes (a fixed share of the event), percent (of what the
minutes leave), or neither (the remaining time, what the minutes and
percents leave); remaining true gives one with minutes or percent the
remaining time too. The minutes must fit in
the event, and the percents add up to no more than 100; read back,
minutes are cut to fit an event shortened since, and goals deleted
since are left out. Set them to replace them whole ([] for none).
Most events have none: tag an event with a goal only when that goal
was open (inactive or active) when the event started -- open now, or
closed after it started -- and the event clearly matches its
attribution_hints, or with none its title -- never guess. Tag the
most specific goal that fits (a sub-goal rather than its parent), and
give minutes or percent when only part of the event was for it.

facts are what compaction established about a past event, for
traits' judgments later: location_ids (see
get_locations), with_ids (the people there with the user -- never
"self", who's at every event), for_ids (people it was done for who
weren't there), notes ({person id: a subjective note on how it was
for them}, "self" for the user) and commute (true for getting from
one place to another). Compaction writes them; set them to replace
them whole. Each place and person can take a share of the event:
{location_id or person_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?} in place of
the id -- minutes (a fixed share), percent (of what the minutes leave),
and remaining true for the rest too. One given as a bare id takes the
remaining time, what the minutes and percents leave: each person all of
it, and the places an even part each. Each list's minutes must fit in
the event, and its percents add up to no more than 100. with_ids and
for_ids can name circles (get_circles) too, by id or as {circle_id,
except?, minutes?, percent?, remaining?}: a plain circle (kind
"circle") stands for its members now, each there (or it for each)
unless except names them, each taking its share whole, as a person
does; a community stands for itself, none of its members assumed, so
list those there too, and it takes no except. Notes and logs are for
the people there, a plain circle's members included; no one is both
with and for, through a circle or not.

judgments are how the event went for each person, judged after
compaction against each judgment part of the traits that apply to them
(see record_judgments): {person id: {trait id: {part key: {"rating",
"scale", "reasoning"}}}}. Set them to overwrite a rating by hand
(replacing them whole), or clear them.

repeat is write-only: given to create_event, or to update_event for an
event that isn't in a series, it makes the event the first of a
recurring series that repeats as it says (see Repeat), in the
calendar's time zone. The event's id becomes the series' own, and the
series' events (list_events) each get their own id, with the series'
as their recurring_event_id. It's never returned: get_recurrence says
how a series repeats, and update_recurrence changes it.

Everything before the last compaction (get_compaction_status's
last_compaction) is history: see update_event.

description_format.description:
How description is written: plain, html or markdown -- markdown
for what you write. None, it's HTML if it has tags, else plain
text. Google Calendar shows a description as it is, whatever its
format; clearing description clears it too.

anyOf.description: An action's id: it takes an even part of the remaining time, what the minutes and percents leave.

etag.description:
Which version of the event this is, as Calendar gives it; it
changes whenever the event does. Give it to update_event and delete_event -- the etag you last read: without it, the change is refused; changed since, the call is refused with every event that's changed, as it is now (_meta.conflicts) -- on a conflict, read it again: if what changed elsewhere is in fields you aren't changing, make your change again on it as it is now; if it's in fields you're changing, or it was deleted (or, deleting it, it was changed since), stop and ask the user -- showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite their change, or put back what was deleted, without their OK.

every.description:
How often the series repeats: its events fall in every `interval`th
day, week, month or year.

interval.description:
1 for every day/week/month/year, 2 for every other one, and so on.
At least 1.

weekdays.description:
The days of the week events fall on, e.g. ["mon", "wed"]. Mostly
for `every` "week". With "day" it keeps only those days (every
weekday: "week" with all five is clearer); with "month" or "year"
it's every one of those weekdays in the month or year -- use
`nth_weekdays` for "the first Monday".

nth_weekdays.description:
Particular weekdays of the month, like the first Monday or the last
Friday. Only for `every` "month", or "year" with `months` set (each
then counts within those months). Can be given with `weekdays`.

month_days.description:
The days of the month events fall on: 1 to 31, or -1 for the last
day (months without a given day are skipped, so use -1 for "the end
of the month", not 31). Not for `every` "week".

months.description:
Only these months, 1 (January) to 12 (December). Mostly for `every`
"year", e.g. [11] with `nth_weekdays` for the 4th Thursday of
November.

count.description:
End the series after this many events, counting from its first.
Can't be given with `until`; give neither for a series that never
ends.

until.description:
End the series here: no event starts after it. A date ("2026-12-31")
means through the end of that day, in the series' time zone; a
datetime is exact. Can't be given with `count`.

week_starts_on.description:
The day weeks start on, which only matters for `every` "week" with
an `interval` above 1 and several `weekdays`: it decides which days
count as the same week. Monday when left out.

skipped.description:
Starts of events the series leaves out, e.g.
["2026-11-09T09:00:00-05:00"]. Each must be exactly the start the
rules give that event (a time without an offset is taken to be in the
series' time zone). (To cancel one event, cancelling it through
update_event is usually simpler.)

added.description:
Starts of extra events, beyond those the rules make, e.g.
["2026-12-01T14:00:00-05:00"] (a time without an offset is taken to
be in the series' time zone). Each lasts as long as the series'
events do.

description:
Change several events at once, as one batch: `updates` (each an
event's id and the fields to set -- left out, a field keeps its value;
list it in that update's clear_fields to remove it instead -- clearing
priority makes it follow its actions' and goals' again), `creates` (new
events, optionally with actions: action_ids, the first setting its
color), `cancels` (each saying whether it counts against
follow-through: a commitment dropped, rather than a change of plan --
see delete_event). An event can be in only one of them; to move
events, update each with its new times. Set action_ids to change an event's actions ([] for none), and
facts to replace its facts whole (see list_events). An update can't
cancel an event (is_cancelled): put it in `cancels`.
WHERE an event is (facts.location_ids), when you set it: keep a
location it already has unless the events and notes around it
clearly show the user was somewhere else. Otherwise the user stays
put: it's where the previous event was, unless there's evidence they
moved in between -- the previous event, or one between, is a commute
(an action with commute true, see get_actions, or the commute fact);
the user said they were somewhere other than planned; or the event
clearly matches another location's hint (see get_locations). After a
commute they're somewhere other than before it: tell where from the
location of the event after it (that one event only), or else from
the locations' hints. A commute itself gets the commute fact and no
location_ids.

GOALS an event is for (goals), when you set them: only goals that
were open (inactive or active) when the event started -- open now, or
closed (closed_at, see get_goals) after it started -- and only when
the event clearly matches a goal's attribution_hints, or with none
its title -- never guess, and leave an event untagged when it's
unclear (or when the user asks, tag it as they say). Tag
the most specific goal that fits, a sub-goal rather than its parent,
and when only part of the event was for it, give minutes or percent.

Set repeat, on a create or on an update of an event that isn't in a
series, to make it the first event of a recurring series (see
PublicEvent); only that first event is checked for overlaps, as for
update_recurrence. An update can't be of a series itself (the id a
series' events give as recurring_event_id) -- edit it with
update_recurrence -- nor give repeat to an event already in one.

BATCHES ARE CHECKED WHOLE, AND NOTHING IS MOVED TO MAKE ROOM: every
event the call creates or updates must end after it starts and must
not overlap any other event -- one on the calendar or another in the
call -- so move, shorten or cancel whatever's in the way in the same
call. A call that breaks this changes nothing, and the error lists
every problem and the events around them, to send a valid call at
once.

VERSIONS: each update and cancel gives the event's etag as you last
read it (list_events and get_event give it). One without is refused;
one changed since is refused, with every such event as it is now
(_meta.conflicts). Then read each again: if what changed elsewhere is
in fields you aren't changing, make your change again on it as it is
now; if it's in fields you're changing, or it was deleted or cancelled
(or, cancelling it, it was changed since), stop and ask the user --
showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite
their change, or put back what was deleted, without their OK. Calendar
writes each event on its own, so one changed after the batch is
checked stops it partway: the error says which changes were written
(_meta.partly) before it stopped. Sending the batch again, from what's
there now, is safe -- what was written is given as it is -- except a
create made without an id of its own, which would be made again:
leave those out.

Everything before the last compaction (get_compaction_status's
last_compaction) is history: an event that started before it can't be
changed or cancelled, and no event can be created, or moved, to start
before it, unless allow_compacted_changes is set -- ONLY set it when
the user has explicitly approved changing history -- except that an
event still going on then may run on (an update moving only its end,
to no earlier than the last compaction). dry_run checks the batch
and returns what it would do without changing anything. Returns the
events changed, and a timeline of them beside the events around
them.

description:

every one of its events, past ones and any edited on their own
included. Or, with starting_at_event_id, delete that event and the
ones after it only ("this and following"): the series is ended just
before it, and the events before it are kept as they are. To delete
one event of a series, use delete_event with that event's id instead.
Returns what's left of the series: nothing if it was deleted whole
(or from its first event on), else the series, now ending before the
event.

The two leave different things behind. Deleting a series whole
cancels each of its events, as delete_event does one: they stay on
the calendar as cancelled events, hidden from the user and from
list_events -- past events too, whose time is then no longer counted
as spent. Deleting this and following leaves no
cancelled events: the series' events from that one on are gone (one
edited on its own goes by where the series first put it, even if
moved earlier). Neither counts against follow-through: only an event
the user cancelled does (see delete_event). To stop
a series that's already begun -- one that won't happen any more,
rather than one that shouldn't have been -- delete from its next
event on.

description:
Create new events, as one batch, optionally with actions
(action_ids, the first setting its color) and facts. update_event
takes creates too, beside updates and cancels, for a change that
makes room for them. An event given a repeat is the first of a new
recurring series (see PublicEvent); only it is checked for overlaps,
not the series' later events.
WHERE an event is (facts.location_ids), when you set it: keep a
location it already has unless the events and notes around it
clearly show the user was somewhere else. Otherwise the user stays
put: it's where the previous event was, unless there's evidence they
moved in between -- the previous event, or one between, is a commute
(an action with commute true, see get_actions, or the commute fact);
the user said they were somewhere other than planned; or the event
clearly matches another location's hint (see get_locations). After a
commute they're somewhere other than before it: tell where from the
location of the event after it (that one event only), or else from
the locations' hints. A commute itself gets the commute fact and no
location_ids.

GOALS an event is for (goals), when you set them: only goals that
were open (inactive or active) when the event started -- open now, or
closed (closed_at, see get_goals) after it started -- and only when
the event clearly matches a goal's attribution_hints, or with none
its title -- never guess, and leave an event untagged when it's
unclear (or when the user asks, tag it as they say). Tag
the most specific goal that fits, a sub-goal rather than its parent,
and when only part of the event was for it, give minutes or percent.

BATCHES ARE CHECKED WHOLE, AND NOTHING IS MOVED TO MAKE ROOM: every
event the call creates or updates must end after it starts and must
not overlap any other event -- one on the calendar or another in the
call -- so move, shorten or cancel whatever's in the way in the same
call. A call that breaks this changes nothing, and the error lists
every problem and the events around them, to send a valid call at
once.

An event can't be created to start before the last compaction
(get_compaction_status's last_compaction): that's history, unless
allow_compacted_changes is set -- ONLY set it when the user has
explicitly approved changing history. dry_run checks them and returns
what it would do without changing anything. Returns the events created, and a timeline of them beside
the events around them.

etag.description:
Which version of the event this is, as Calendar gives it; it
changes whenever the event does. Give it to update_event and delete_event -- the etag you last read: without it, the change is refused; changed since, the call is refused with every event that's changed, as it is now (_meta.conflicts) -- on a conflict, read it again: if what changed elsewhere is in fields you aren't changing, make your change again on it as it is now; if it's in fields you're changing, or it was deleted (or, deleting it, it was changed since), stop and ask the user -- showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite their change, or put back what was deleted, without their OK.

every.description:
How often the series repeats: its events fall in every `interval`th
day, week, month or year.

interval.description:
1 for every day/week/month/year, 2 for every other one, and so on.
At least 1.

weekdays.description:
The days of the week events fall on, e.g. ["mon", "wed"]. Mostly
for `every` "week". With "day" it keeps only those days (every
weekday: "week" with all five is clearer); with "month" or "year"
it's every one of those weekdays in the month or year -- use
`nth_weekdays` for "the first Monday".

nth_weekdays.description:
Particular weekdays of the month, like the first Monday or the last
Friday. Only for `every` "month", or "year" with `months` set (each
then counts within those months). Can be given with `weekdays`.

month_days.description:
The days of the month events fall on: 1 to 31, or -1 for the last
day (months without a given day are skipped, so use -1 for "the end
of the month", not 31). Not for `every` "week".

months.description:
Only these months, 1 (January) to 12 (December). Mostly for `every`
"year", e.g. [11] with `nth_weekdays` for the 4th Thursday of
November.

count.description:
End the series after this many events, counting from its first.
Can't be given with `until`; give neither for a series that never
ends.

until.description:
End the series here: no event starts after it. A date ("2026-12-31")
means through the end of that day, in the series' time zone; a
datetime is exact. Can't be given with `count`.

week_starts_on.description:
The day weeks start on, which only matters for `every` "week" with
an `interval` above 1 and several `weekdays`: it decides which days
count as the same week. Monday when left out.

skipped.description:
Starts of events the series leaves out, e.g.
["2026-11-09T09:00:00-05:00"]. Each must be exactly the start the
rules give that event (a time without an offset is taken to be in the
series' time zone). (To cancel one event, cancelling it through
update_event is usually simpler.)

added.description:
Starts of extra events, beyond those the rules make, e.g.
["2026-12-01T14:00:00-05:00"] (a time without an offset is taken to
be in the series' time zone). Each lasts as long as the series'
events do.

description:
The traits: how the user wants to be with people (and with
themselves), in order -- by default the active ones (rated) and those
turned off (kept, but not rated for now), not archived ones
(retired). Each has an id (fixed when it's created, and what a
person's traits name), name, definition, parts and scoring. Each part
is {"id": ..., "kind": ..., "engagement_type": "with", ...}: id is the
part's own, made when it's added and never changed -- its judgments and
weight are kept under it, so keep it on a part you send back, and leave
it out of a new one; engagement_type "with" (the default) reads the
events the person was at with the user, "for" those the user did for
them while they weren't there. A trait's score (0-100) combines its
parts' scores as its scoring says, leaving out any with nothing to rate
it by: without scoring, their plain mean. Scoring is an aggregation,
as are a person's and a circle's (see get_scoring_defaults for its
fields): a trait's weights are by part id, {"weights": {"<part id>":
2}} counting that part twice. The kinds:
"judgment" -- each event judged by the assistant on its own, never by
asking the user, for one person or a named group, against a "rubric"
(the question: "Was this activity or place new?") on a scale of
"ratings" ({"0": "The activity and place were routine", "1": "There
was a twist on the activity or place", "2": "The activity or the
place were new", "3": "Both were new, or it was otherwise
adventurous"}), from the "facts" it names: "action" (what was done),
"action_history" (what's been done with them before), "location",
"location_history" (where they've been together before),
"general_notes" (the event's notes) and any of the trait's own facts
as "fact:<fact id>" (its summary of the person, as it is now), each a
name or {"fact": "action_history", "lookback_days": 90} (history facts
look back 30 days by default),
and scored over the person's events in its last "window_days" (30
by default) as its "scoring" says: {"weight_by": "event" (each
judgment counts once, the default) or "duration" (each by its event's
length), "statistic": "mean" (the default) or "percentile" (with
"percentile": 0-100 -- the lowest rating with at least that share of
the judgments, or of their time, at or below it; 0 the lowest, 100 the
highest), "limit" and "limit_by": only the judgments of the "best"
(highest rated), "worst" or most "recent" limit events, or -- weighted
by duration -- limit hours, the last event cut short to fit};
"continuity" (the last event ended within "last_within_days" of the
day's end and the next starts within "next_within_days" after it,
both default 14: 100 for both, 50 for one, 0 for neither); "count"
({"kind": "count", "target": 1, "interval_days": 21, "zero_at_days":
42, "noun": "visits"}), "duration" (with "target_min") and
"follow_through" ("penalty", "recovery", "look_back_days"), as the
measures of the same kind -- follow_through counting the events the
user cancelled: said in compaction didn't happen, or deleted with
delete_event's counts_against_follow_through, never a plan merely
changed; "spacing" ({"kind": "spacing", "action": "<meals>",
"max_gap_hours": 6, "exceptions": [{"actions": ["<sleep>"],
"reset_hours": 1}]}): a clock that each event of its action resets to
max_gap_hours left, stopped during an exception's events and, after
one, set to its reset_hours left (if given) -- each day scored as
the share of its time outside exceptions that the clock hadn't run
out; "schedule" ({"kind": "schedule", "action": "<work>", "from":
"10:00", "to": "18:00", "measure": "covered", "days": ["mon", "tue",
"wed", "thu", "fri"], "window_days": 7, "slack_minutes": 60}): when
its action's events happen -- each day it's on (days, weekdays "mon"
to "sun", by default every day) scored by its window from "from" to
"to" ("HH:MM" in the calendar's time zone; "to" before "from" crosses
midnight) as its measure says: "starts" 100 if an event starts in it,
else 0; "ends" the same for one ending in it; "covered" the share of
it the events cover, slack_minutes (only for covered; 0 by default)
forgiven -- and the part's score of a day the mean of the days it's
on in the window_days (7 by default) ending with it.
continuity, count, duration and follow_through can take an
"action" (an action or action group id) to count only its events. A
trait's facts are what it keeps about each person it applies to, for
its judgments: each {"id", "name", "summary_prompt", "log_prompt"?} --
id made from the name when it's added, and never changed; the
summary_prompt says what its summary of a person keeps, and how
(compaction rewrites a person's summary whole when an event's notes
show something new, logging what changed on the event, as the
log_prompt says). A person's summaries are in get_people's facts, and
the logs in get_fact_logs. A person's traits can select which traits
apply to them, give them their own parts for any, and say how they
combine (see create_person). problems lists anything wrong with a
trait edited by hand; a bad part isn't rated. Read-only.

description:
Add a habit: a name (unique among habits), the action or action
group whose events it's about (action_id: an action's or a group's
id; only events with that action, or any action under that group,
count toward it), and optionally a note (what it's for, and what
doing it well looks like -- context for judging its events) and
traits: {"select": "all" or [trait ids], "parts": {trait id:
[parts]}, "part_scoring": {trait id: scoring}, "scoring": scoring},
all optional, as a person's (see create_person) -- the traits that
apply to it (by default every active one), parts replacing a trait's
for it alone (a more specific rubric, say), and how they combine. It's
always "with": judgment parts for those an event was done "for"
don't apply to it. Also optionally foundations: the habits (each as
"habit:<id>") it's built on -- sleeping well under exercising, say;
none of them deleted, and never making a cycle.
A person's or circle's habit has a person_id or circle_id in place of
action_id: it's some of their traits, scored as they are for them (a
circle's, its people's combined as the circle's scoring says) -- a
layer of the relationship on the habit graph, being reliable for
Sam under being close to them, say. Its traits take only "select"
(the traits it's on; by default all that apply to them) and
"except" (traits left out, though selected: those added later are
on it), and its events aren't judged for it: they're theirs. Its
name is optional: without one it's named by them and its traits
("Sam · Reliable", "Sam · except Reliable"), and it loses its own
when its traits or whose it is change, unless given another (given
its default, it has none of its own: default_name lists it).
A recurring goal's habit has a recurring_goal in place of action_id:
{period: day | week | month | quarter | year, title?, priority?, expected_minutes?,
description?, definition_of_done?, attribution_hints?, with_ids?,
for_ids?, rate_periods?} -- a goal for each period on the calendar
(weeks run Sunday to Saturday, quarters from January), made by the server as each begins,
once the one before is done or obsolete, and tried again through the
next period when it's missed; titled by the habit's name unless it
gives one. Its goals have its id and the period's start as theirs
("<habit id>_2026-11-01") and are its (habit_id); its events are
those tagged with them. It's scored by its goal rate -- the share of
its last rate_periods periods (by default 7 days, 6 weeks, 4 months,
4 quarters or 2 years) with a goal done -- and
by its traits only once given some (it's made with {"select": []}).
Archived or deleted, its open goal is made obsolete.
Active unless given a status. id is assigned. Returns the habit and
its id as created_id.

description:
The user's goals: outcomes they mean to reach and can mark done (not
ongoing practices -- those are habits). By default the inactive and
active ones, not done, missed or obsolete ones; every depth, each with its
parent_id and path (its parents' titles, outermost first). A goal
can sit under another to any depth: a sub-goal is a piece of reaching
its parent, and required says whether its parent needs it done.
A priority (0 the most, as actions'; optional) says how much it
matters: without one, a goal takes its nearest parent's that has one,
and with none up its tree it's treated as 3. A background_color
(#rrggbb; optional) colors it in the app: without one, a goal takes
its nearest parent's that has one, and with none up its tree, its
priority's (see get_priority_colors); effective_color is its own or
the parent's it takes, none when it's its priority's. sort_order (optional)
is the user's own order among goals that otherwise list alike (the
same priority, due the same day): the lowest first, those without one
after them; leave it as it is unless asked to reorder goals.
Each has a title, an optional expected_minutes (how long it's
expected to take: a guide for comparing with the time spent, never
enforced), a deadline -- {at: "2026-11-01"} (due at the end of that
day) or {at: "2026-11-01T17:00"}, in the calendar's time zone; or
measured from something, and kept so while it's open: {before_parent:
{days | minutes}} (that far before its parent's; moving it to the top
level unties it), {after_start: {days | minutes}} (after it becomes
active: days, the end of that many days after the day it started) or
{after_goal: {id, days | minutes}} (after another goal's) -- and due,
when that falls ("2026-11-01" or "2026-11-01T17:00"; none until one
measured from its start starts). Every open goal needs a deadline,
and an active one a due. An inactive goal can wait to be activated
(activate_when): {after: [{goal_closed: id} (done, missed or
obsolete) | {at: a date or a date and time}] -- every one -- then
delay: "next_day" (the start of the day after) or {minutes}, and
hold_while: [{active_at_least: n, priority?: {at_or_above | exactly:
a priority or "own"}}] (held back while that many other goals of that
priority are active, its own parents and sub-goals not counted)}.
Ready and not held, it's activated -- dated when it became ready --
with its inactive parents; activating it by hand ignores it, and
either way it's cleared -- as it is when the goal is closed (done,
missed or obsolete) while it waits. expected_start is when one waiting is
expected to be: when what it waits for is due, then its delay; none
while it's held, or what it waits for has no due yet. A status (inactive, active, done, missed -- its
deadline passed without it -- or obsolete) and its history (each change of
status and when, oldest first, each with the deadline in force at
that change, if it had one, and a note, if one was left with it --
why it was marked done, say; started_at is when it first became
active, closed_at when it was done, missed or made obsolete). A missed
goal can be reopened with a new deadline, and its history keeps each
deadline it missed, so a goal can be missed and retried any number
of times. Then a description and definition_of_done, each with its
format (description_format, definition_of_done_format: plain, html or
markdown; none, it's HTML if it has tags, else plain text -- write
yours in Markdown, and say so), and attribution_hints (a guide for
telling which events are for it).
with_ids are the people it's done with (who the user works on it
alongside) and for_ids those it's done for, who aren't part of doing
it (a promise to them, a gift, a favor): person ids from get_people,
never "self", and no one in both -- or circles from get_circles: a
plain circle's id for all its members, {circle_id, except: [person
ids]} for all but those, and a community's for the community itself.
A plain circle's member can't be in one while their circle is in the
other.
Events are tagged with goals, apart from their actions (see
list_events' goals): tag an event with a goal only when the goal was
open (inactive or active) when the event started -- open now, or
closed_at after it started -- and the event clearly matches its
attribution_hints, or with none its title -- never guess -- and
with the most specific goal that fits (a sub-goal rather than its
parent). Read-only.
name: get_goals

parent_id (the goal it's a piece of), required, priority, background_color,
expected_minutes, activate_when, description, definition_of_done
(each with its format: markdown for yours), attribution_hints,
with_ids and for_ids. Active unless given a
status; activating a goal activates its inactive parents. Its history
starts with its status, now, unless given one (to backdate it, say).
A sub-goal can't be due after its parent, or be expected to take
longer, or be open (inactive or active) under a done, missed or
obsolete one. A goal can't wait, through others, for itself, or for a
parent to close, and a deadline can't be measured, through others,
from its own. id is assigned
unless given (a client's own, so it can name the goal before it's
made; the same create sent again gives the goal as it was made).
Returns the goal and its id as created_id.

ActivateWhen.description:
What an inactive goal waits for before the server activates it: every
trigger in after (none, it's ready now), then the delay, if any; and
while any of hold_while holds, it waits on. Activated, by the server or
by hand (which ignores it), it's cleared -- as it is when the goal is
closed while it waits.

CircleExcept.description: A plain circle named with those of its members who aren't part of it.

except.description: Those of its members who aren't, by person id.

Deadline.description:
A goal's deadline as set: exactly one of at (a date, "2026-11-01", due
at the end of that day, or a date and time, "2026-11-01T17:00", in the
calendar's time zone), before_parent (that far before its parent's
deadline), after_start (that far after it becomes active) or
after_goal (that far after another goal's deadline). One measured from
something is kept so while the goal is open: its due follows what it's
measured from. One measured from its start has no due until the goal
starts, and keeps the one it gets then.

DelayMinutes.description: A wait of this many minutes.

GoalInput.description: A goal as create_goal and update_goals take it (see get_goals).

parent_id.description: The goal it's a piece of; none for a top-level goal.

required.description: Whether its parent needs it done to be done.

priority.description:
How much it matters, 0 the most, as actions' priorities; none, it
takes its nearest parent's that has one, and with none up its tree,

background_color.description:
Its color, as "#rrggbb" (e.g. "#a4bdfc"); none, it takes its
nearest parent's that has one, or else its priority's (see

sort_order.description:

expected_minutes.description:

deadline.description:

description:
Change goals, all at once, checked whole: `updates` (each a goal's id
and the fields to set -- left out, a field keeps its value; list it in
that update's clear_fields to remove it instead), `creates` (new goals,
as create_goal takes them; an update can name one by an id given
here) and `deletes`. A status set without a history adds the change,
now, with the goal's deadline after the change, and the update's
status_note, to the goal's history; a history given replaces it whole
(to backdate a change, or remove a
mistaken one), its entries' deadlines as given, and must end with the
goal's status. To retry a missed goal, set its new deadline and give
its history ending missed (with the deadline it missed) then active or
inactive (with the new one), both at the same moment -- how the app
records a retry.

The rules (see get_goals and create_goal) hold for the result, not
for each step: to mark a goal done, missed or obsolete, close or move its
open sub-goals in the same call; to delete one, delete or move its
sub-goals too; to make an earlier deadline fit, change its sub-goals'
in the same call. Nothing is moved or changed to make things fit: a
call that breaks a rule changes nothing, and the error names the goals
in the way. Deleting a goal can't be undone; events tagged with it
stop showing it. Give each update its version, and each delete its if_version -- the versions you last read (get_goals gives them): without, it's refused; changed since, the call is refused with every goal that's changed, as it is now (_meta.conflicts) -- on a conflict, read it again: if what changed elsewhere is in fields you aren't changing, make your change again on it as it is now; if it's in fields you're changing, or it was deleted (or, deleting it, it was changed since), stop and ask the user -- showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite their change, or put back what was deleted, without their OK. Returns each goal made or
changed, as it is now, and the ids deleted.

description:
How scores combine wherever nothing says otherwise -- the defaults the
user's app scores by: traits (how a person's or habit's traits combine
into their score, unless their traits' own scoring says), circles (how
a circle's people combine into its score, unless its own scoring says)
and habit_layers (how the habits and people in each layer of the habit
graph combine into the layer's score). Each is an aggregation, or null
for the plain mean -- for habit_layers, the lowest score. An aggregation -- this, a trait's scoring, a
person's or habit's traits' scoring and part_scoring, and a circle's
scoring -- is an object with any of: "statistic": "mean" (weighted;
the default) or "percentile" (with "percentile": 0-100 -- the lowest
score with at least that share of the weight at or below it, so 0 is
the lowest score and 100 the highest); "weights": {id: weight, 0 or
more} (each 1 unless given; ids as the level says -- part ids, trait
ids, person ids, or "habit:<id>" for habits); "limit" (a whole number)
and "limit_by": "best" or "worst" -- only the limit highest or lowest
scores count; "cap_below": {"threshold": score, "cap": score} -- with
any score under threshold, the result is at most cap; and "missing":
"skip" (the default: what has nothing to rate it by is left out) or a
score to count it as. Scores are 0-100. Read-only.

description:

nearest it (`remaining_note_count` says how many are left for another
round) -- those days' planned events, a `timeline` showing the two
side by side, day by day, and instructions. Compare the notes to the
plan, decide which events the notes show happened differently, and
the facts of each past event -- its actions, where it was, who was
there, who it was for, and a note on each person there -- then call
compact_notes with those decisions. Also every action an event can be
given (`actions`, their groups left out), every person (`people`, the
user as "self", each with their trait facts' summaries) and every
location (`locations`), to settle the facts from; each trait fact,
described once (`trait_facts`), to keep people's summaries by; and the
goals to tag events with (`goals`: the open ones, and those closed
since the earliest event started, with `closed_at` -- each to tag an
event with when it clearly matches its hints, or with none its title,
a closed one only on events that started before it closed; one with
`due_in_window` had its deadline pass inside the window, to propose
missed with compact_notes' `goal_changes` unless something shows it
done).
`proposal` is the open proposal, if there is one: revise or
extend it (see the instructions). judgments_pending names the last
compaction if its judgments aren't all made: make them first
(prepare_judgments, record_judgments). Read-only.

instructions.default: `timeline` shows the notes beside the planned events -- for every day of notes up to now, each under a heading with its date (`days` lists them when there's more than one). Each day is compacted on its own, but you decide them all in one list. Compare them and decide, event by event, what the notes show happened differently -- then call compact_notes with them, as `updates`, `creates` and `cancels`. SILENCE MEANS ON SCHEDULE: any past event you don't mention is recorded exactly as planned, so only mention the events the notes contradict. Notes are sparse -- the user doesn't note every event, so a missing start or end note never means an event didn't happen or ran into its neighbor. READ EACH NOTE'S TENSE to tell which edge it marks: most notes are written as something finishes, so a note in the past tense ('finished the report', 'had lunch', 'done with email', 'went for a walk') marks the END of that event -- it ran up to the note's time, not from it. Only a note in the future tense ('going to the gym', 'will start the report', 'about to eat') or one that explicitly says it's starting something ('starting email', 'heading out to', 'now working on') marks a START. Don't assume a note starts the event it names; when the tense is ambiguous (a bare 'email'), use the timing and the neighboring notes, and ask if it's still unclear. `updates` {event_id}: it happened; each edge stays as planned unless you move it -- {start_note}/{end_note} (a note id) sets that edge to the note's time and links the note to it, {start}/{end} sets an explicit time (add the note too when it gives a time relative to itself, e.g. 'leaving 15 minutes early'). An update also takes {summary} to rename an event and {annotate} to add text to its description. `creates` {summary, a start and an end (a time or note each), action_ids?, facts?}: something unplanned happened. `cancels` {event_id, counts_against_follow_through}: it didn't happen -- true if the user dropped it (skipped it, didn't get to it: it counts against the follow-through of whoever it was planned with), false if the plan changed for another reason (someone else called it off, it moved elsewhere). An event goes in only one of the lists. When the user tells you they don't remember where one event ended and the next began, grow one with an update (renamed after both) and cancel the other, not counting it -- only then, never just because the notes are sparse. NOTHING IS MOVED TO MAKE ROOM: every event you update or create must end after it starts and must not overlap any other event in `events` -- past or still to come, the others you change included. When a moved edge runs into a neighbor, move, shorten or cancel the neighbor in the same call (an overrun usually delays or shortens the next event; ask the user if the notes don't say which gives way). A call that breaks this changes nothing, and lists every problem and the day as it would leave it, so fix them all at once. Every note has its text added to the description of an event: one you use as an end_note to the event it ends, else one used as a start_note to the event it starts, and any other to the event it falls within; list any that shouldn't be in `ignore_notes` (an edge note there still sets its edge), and any that belong with another event in `annotate_notes` ({note_id, event_id} -- an event's id, or a create's `key` from the open proposal; for a new create, put the text in its `annotate`). Use only note ids from `notes` (only this round's -- a longer backlog than this takes another round, see `remaining_note_count`) and event ids from `events`. `events` may start with one that ended just before `compaction_window_start` (usually last night's sleep); if a note shows it actually ran later -- the user slept in -- move its end with an update, and say when whatever it now overlaps happened. An event with `history_until` was settled by an earlier compaction up to then -- usually one still going on when it ran: its start, and its lasting until then, are fact, so keep its start, end it no earlier (it may well have run later), and don't cancel it; compact_notes refuses otherwise. Likewise, what's still going on now is recorded up to now, and the next compaction says where it ended. Each round starts where the last one stopped, at `compaction_window_start`, and runs to `now`, however much of a day that is: when the last one ran in the evening, notes written during the planned night mean the user stayed up -- move the night's start (bedtime) to when they went to bed. `previous_note`, if there is one, is the last note an earlier compaction already used, however long ago -- context only (it can't be used as a start_note/end_note or ignored): e.g. if it said 'starting the report' shortly before `compaction_window_start`, the report was already under way as this window began, and the first note may well be its end; the longer before the window it was written, the less it says about how the window began. The timeline shows it too (✓), and when the last compaction ran, both as context. COMPACTION RECORDS THE PAST: `events` runs on a little past `now` (to `day_end`), but `timeline` stops at `now`, except for later events near a note (one may be what a note starts early) and, once proposed, later events the plan changes. An update that moves a future event reschedules it -- for 'move lunch later and adjust the afternoon': move each event it now runs into too, in the same call. A night's sleep is an event like any other: moving its start moves bedtime (an earlier one needs whatever runs past it shortened or cancelled in the same call), and its end is the wake-up time. A note that marks waking up (early or late) is that night's end_note; a note in the night that doesn't end it ('can't sleep') is just added to it. If the user slept in, the morning events the night now runs over -- past or still to come, even past this round's now -- have to be moved, shortened or cancelled in the same call. Cancel a night only if the user didn't sleep. COMPACTION ESTABLISHES THE FACTS of every past event, which traits are judged from later -- so for each past event in the timeline, settle: what the user was doing (its ACTIONS), where it was, who was there with them, who it was for, and a note on each person who was there. Settle them from the notes, the title and the description; don't ask the user what the notes already say, and leave out what doesn't apply (a solo event has no `with_ids`). ACTIONS: each event's `action_ids` are what the user was doing, each a verb from `actions` ("play guitar", "eat a meal"); an event can have several, the first setting its color. Each is an id -- an even part of the remaining time, what the minutes and percents leave -- or {action_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?} when the notes say how long it took (remaining: true for its part of the remaining time as well). For every past event with `suggested_action_ids`, add an update {event_id, action_ids} applying them unless the notes say otherwise; give a create its action_ids too. When no action fits, add one (see NEW below) rather than force a poor match. An update without action_ids keeps them, and [] clears them. In the timeline, ◆ marks an action an event already has and ◇ one it's being given (or, before deciding, one suggested). FACTS: add `facts` to the event's update (or create): location_ids (from `locations`, matched by their hints -- usually one; several when it moved between places), with_ids (people from `people` who were there; never "self" -- the user is at every event), for_ids (people it was done for who weren't there: preparing a gift or a plan -- then they're not in with_ids) -- either can name a circle from `circles` too: a plain one (kind circle) stands for its members, so name it when the group was there, as {circle_id, except: [the person ids of any of it who weren't]} if some weren't; a community stands for itself, so name it when the user was at the group's own thing (a social, a meetup), and list the people they actually spent time with there too; a community has trait facts of its own (its `facts` in `circles`), kept, logged and summarized exactly as a person's -- and notes: {person id: a subjective line on how it was for them} for each person who was there, "self" for the user -- whatever the notes say that might help judge it later (they were tired, it was their idea, we laughed a lot). The notes aren't judgments: you don't know the traits, so just record what happened. Facts replace an event's facts whole, so an event that has some (`facts`) keeps them unless you send new ones. In the timeline, ▸ marks facts an event has and ▹ ones it's being given. Once proposed, ⚠ marks a past event still missing its action or location (listed again under `Missing:` at the end of the day): settle it from the notes and propose again, or, if they don't say, ask the user -- or, with no one to ask (a scheduled run), leave it for the user to settle in review. GOALS: `goals` lists the open goals (inactive or active) that have attribution hints -- the only ones to tag events with. Tag a past event with a goal (its update's or create's `goals`: [{goal_id, minutes?, percent?}]) only when the event clearly matches that goal's `attribution_hints`; never guess for a goal that isn't listed (one without hints, or one done, missed or obsolete), and leave an event untagged when it's unclear. Tag the most specific goal that fits -- a sub-goal (its `path` names its parents) rather than its parent. When only part of the event was for the goal, give minutes (a fixed share) or percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining: true if it also takes the remaining time; with neither, it takes the remaining time (what the minutes and percents leave). An event can be for several goals. Goals replace an event's goals whole: an update without goals keeps them, and [] clears them. NEW actions, people and locations: when an event's action, a person or a place isn't in the lists, add it with compact_notes' new_actions, new_people or new_locations -- each with a `ref` starting "new:" ("new:ukulele") that your updates and creates use wherever its id would go -- rather than by separate tools: they're created when the plan is applied, so the user confirms them with it. A new action is a verb phrase, its status active (the user approves it with the plan); a new person needs a context when their name is taken; a new location needs a hint. Check the lists first: don't add one that's already there under another name. In a conversation, confirm with the user anything you couldn't settle from the notes -- who was there, where it was -- in a short list before proposing; with no one to ask, propose what the notes do say. The user confirms the whole proposal, in the app. In a conversation, after every compact_notes show the user the result's `timeline.text` verbatim in a code block (it's laid out narrow enough for a phone, so don't reformat or widen it -- it shows each event's actions and facts compactly, under it), then the new actions, people and locations it adds, and the warnings. RECAP: every compact_notes call takes your `recap` of the proposal, which the user reads beside it in the app: a short `overview`; `did`, one point for each thing you decided (what, and from which notes); and `unsure`, one point for each thing you're not sure of, saying what you assumed and what would settle it (empty only if nothing is in doubt -- don't pad it). Each point is Markdown (bold, italics, code, bullet and numbered lists; no headings or tables), and cites the events (`event_ids`: ids, keys, or the `ref` you give a create) and notes (`note_ids`) it's about, so the user can go straight to them. Don't restate the timeline: say what a reader couldn't see from it. Write it afresh for every revision, about the proposal as it then stands; feedback answers go in `replies`. PROPOSALS: compact_notes doesn't apply anything -- it writes a proposal (or a new revision of the open one) for the user to review in the app, where they confirm it, edit it, or leave you feedback. With a proposal open (`proposal`), every compact_notes call revises it: pass its proposal_id and the revision you started from, and send ALL your decisions again -- `proposal.updates`, `creates` and `cancels` are your current ones; keep each create's `key` so the user's edits of it follow it -- changed as the notes and the feedback say, planned to now. The user's own edits (`proposal.user_edits`) are laid over yours by the server: never send them, and don't fight them -- that includes what they said a note is for (an edit with action `note`), and the additions they settled (`proposal.settled_additions`: created, found among those there, or dropped -- name each by its `id` from then on, or leave it out; send `proposal.new_actions`, `new_people` and `new_locations` again for the rest). Answer every open feedback item (`proposal.feedback`, status open) in `replies`, saying what you changed, or asking what they meant if you can't tell; to change an event (or a note) the user edited, the feedback you answer has to be about that event (`event_id`) or note (`note_id`). Nothing is applied until the user confirms it, in the app (confirm_proposal isn't yours to call). If they ask you for changes, make them with compact_notes again, passing proposal_id and the revision you started from.

description:
Step 2 of compacting notes: propose what happened -- each day's
events realigned to its notes, and the calendar changes that makes --
for the user to review and confirm in the app. Nothing on the calendar
changes, and you can't apply it: only the user's confirmation does.
Every day since the last compaction is planned together, as one span;
one call covers them all, to now.

Call with what the notes show happened differently from the plan, as
update_event takes a batch (see prepare_compaction's instructions):
`updates` (events that happened, with edges moved to a time or a
note's, renamed, annotated, their actions, goals and facts set),
`creates` (something unplanned that happened) and `cancels` (what
didn't happen, each saying whether it counts against follow-through:
the user dropped it, or the plan changed). Any past event you don't
mention is recorded as on schedule. Tag an event with goals (`goals`,
goal shares as update_event takes them) only from prepare_compaction's
`goals` when it clearly matches a goal's hints, or with none its
title -- a closed goal only if the event started before it closed
(refused otherwise); the most specific goal, with minutes or
percent when only part of it was for the goal. Notes are added to the
event they fall within -- or, one that sets an edge, to the event it
ends, else the one it starts -- except those in `ignore_notes` (which
still set their edges) -- and
those in `annotate_notes`, added to the event they name (an event's
id, a create's key from the open proposal, or its `ref`) instead.
new_actions, new_people and new_locations add what isn't there yet,
each with a `ref` ("new:ukulele") the updates and creates use in
place of its id; they're created when it's applied. new_goals propose
goals -- inactive -- from notes where the user says they want or mean
to do something longer term that no open goal covers, or told someone
they would -- with the people it's with or for (ids, or new_people
refs) -- created when it's applied too. goal_changes propose changes
to goals there are, applied when it's applied: {goal_id, status: done
| missed | obsolete, at?, note_ids?, retry_deadline?} -- `done` at
the note's time when a note says the goal's outcome was reached,
`obsolete` when one says the user dropped it, and `missed` at its
deadline for every goal with `due_in_window` that nothing shows done
(never with a retry_deadline: the user picks that in review). A
change naming a goal that isn't open, timed outside the window, or
that the goal rules refuse (open sub-goals, unless the call closes
them too) is refused, naming the goal. You get the
proposal's id and revision, the proposed changes, the additions, and
a `timeline` of the notes beside the resulting events, each with its
actions and facts -- in a conversation, show its `text` to the user in
a code block, then the additions, the goal changes and the warnings.

`recap` is your account of it, for the user reviewing it in the app:
a short `overview`, then one point for each thing you `did` (what you
decided, and from which notes) and each thing you're `unsure` of
(saying what you assumed -- empty only if nothing is in doubt). Each
point is Markdown (bold, italics, code, lists; no headings) and cites
the events (`event_ids`: ids, keys, or a create's `ref`), the notes
(`note_ids`) and the goal changes (`goal_ids`) it's about, so the user
can go straight to them. Give a
create a `ref` of your choosing to name it before it has a key, here
and in `annotate_notes`. Write it afresh every call, for the proposal
as it now stands.

With a proposal open (prepare_compaction's `proposal`), every call
revises or extends it: pass its `proposal_id` and the `revision` you
started from, send all your decisions again (each create with the
`key` it was given; your goal_changes too, less those the user settled
-- `proposal.settled_goal_changes`), and answer every open feedback item in
`replies`. The user's own edits -- of events, of what notes are
for, and of goal changes -- are laid over your decisions by the server; never send them.

NOTHING IS MOVED TO MAKE ROOM: every event you update or create must
end after it starts and must not overlap any other event -- past or
still to come, the others you change included -- so move, shorten or
cancel whatever's in the way in the same call. A call that breaks this
changes nothing, and the error lists every problem and the day as it
would leave it, to fix them all at once.

An update that moves a future event reschedules it. A night's sleep
is an event like any other: an earlier bedtime needs whatever runs
past it shortened or cancelled too, a later one leaves the evening
free, and a later wake-up has to move, shorten or cancel the morning
events it now runs over, even those after now, in the same call. One
that puts an event past what the round offers takes in the events it
lands among, for the same call to make room among.

fact_summaries rewrite people's trait facts (see prepare_compaction's
`trait_facts`): each {person_id, fact: "<trait id>/<fact id>",
summary} -- the whole summary, as it stands after the proposal's
events -- only beside a log of what changed in the facts of the event
(or events) whose notes showed it ({"logs": {person id: {fact: log}}}),
and every log beside its summary. Change a fact only when the notes
have something relevant to it: most events say nothing new about most
facts.

Once the user confirms it and it's applied, make its judgments with
prepare_judgments and record_judgments: the compaction isn't complete
until they're all recorded.

description:
The user's edits to the open proposal, from the app: `updates`,
`creates` and `cancels` as update_event takes them (an update's id may
be a new event's key), each update and create also taking a
`start_note`/`end_note` that sets that edge. A description given is
the event's whole description, notes and all -- as the proposal
shows it, edited: no notes are added to it. `notes`, what notes are for --
each annotating the event it falls within, or the one named
(`event_id`), or ignored; `additions`, settling an action, person,
location or goal the proposal adds (by its ref) now, without
confirming the rest -- `create` it (with its name -- a goal's title --,
a person's context or a location's hint corrected), say it's one that's `existing` (its id),
or `drop` it from the events; `goal_changes`, settling a goal change
the proposal makes (by its goal's id) now -- `apply` it (an update of
the goal, refused as update_goals would refuse it), `drop` it, or
`change` it, the user's status, `at` and retry_deadline over Claude's,
kept in the proposal (a `change` of a goal the proposal doesn't change
adds one, with a status); and `as_planned` -- events (or keys)
whose decisions to clear, notes to leave as Claude had them, and refs
to leave unsettled. One created or applied stays, whatever becomes of the
proposal. `through`, later than the proposal's, extends it there (no
later than now; it can't be cut short): each note it takes in is added
to the event it falls within, unless `notes` says otherwise, and the
proposal's `claude_through` still says where Claude's revision ran
to.
`revision` is the one the user was looking at. They're laid over the current revision as a new one,
which is returned, with `replaced`: the events whose newer change by
Claude they overrode. If you amend it, give the revision you last read;
when `replaced` names events changed since that revision, or the
proposal moved on so it's refused, read it again: if what changed is
in events you aren't changing, make your edit again on it as it is
now; if it's in events you're changing, stop and ask the user --
showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite
their edit without their OK. Refused, changing nothing, if one names an
event or a note that isn't in the proposal, adds a note to an event
of another day, or the result overlaps, or changes history -- moves
the start of, ends earlier, or cancels an event an earlier compaction
recorded -- unless allow_compacted_changes is set: ONLY set it when the
user has explicitly approved changing history. It's kept with these
edits, so later revisions keep to it. Nothing is moved to make room.
An update or create that puts an event past the proposal's events

PublicEvent.description:
A calendar event, as every event tool takes and returns it.

is_cancelled is read-only: update_event refuses to set it -- cancel
an event with delete_event, which says whether the cancellation counts
against follow-through.

action_ids are what was done at the event (see get_actions), the
first setting its label and color; setting them is how an event is
tied to actions. Each is an action's id, taking an even part of the
remaining time (what the minutes and percents leave), or an object
{action_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?}: minutes (a fixed share),
percent (of what the minutes leave), and remaining true for its part of
the remaining time as well. The minutes must fit in the event and the
percents add up to no more than 100; read back, minutes are cut to fit
an event shortened since. action_names (their names, in the same order) and
event_label_id (derived from the first action) are read-only: an
update ignores them.

actions_from_label is true when an event was never given actions, so
its action_ids are inferred from its label (the action that holds the
label), not stored. Sending it back with actions_from_label still true
leaves them inferred, whatever action_ids says; to store actions, send
action_ids with actions_from_label false (or left out).

effective_priority is read-only: the priority that applies, i.e.
priority falling back,
when the event doesn't set one, to the highest (lowest-numbered)
priority among its actions (each action's own, or its nearest
group's) and its goals (each goal's own, or its nearest parent's, or
else 3). Kept separate from priority so that sending a listed event
straight back to update_event never copies that priority onto the
event itself, which would stop it following later changes to its
actions and goals. An update ignores it.

recurring_event_id is read-only too, and an update ignores it as
well: it's assigned by Google and can't be set at all.

goals are the goals the event is for (see get_goals): each a goal_id,
with minutes (a fixed share of the event), percent (of what the
minutes leave), or neither (the remaining time, what the minutes and
percents leave); remaining true gives one with minutes or percent the
remaining time too. The minutes must fit in
the event, and the percents add up to no more than 100; read back,
minutes are cut to fit an event shortened since, and goals deleted
since are left out. Set them to replace them whole ([] for none).
Most events have none: tag an event with a goal only when that goal
was open (inactive or active) when the event started -- open now, or
closed after it started -- and the event clearly matches its
attribution_hints, or with none its title -- never guess. Tag the
most specific goal that fits (a sub-goal rather than its parent), and
give minutes or percent when only part of the event was for it.

facts are what compaction established about a past event, for
traits' judgments later: location_ids (see
get_locations), with_ids (the people there with the user -- never
"self", who's at every event), for_ids (people it was done for who
weren't there), notes ({person id: a subjective note on how it was
for them}, "self" for the user) and commute (true for getting from
one place to another). Compaction writes them; set them to replace
them whole. Each place and person can take a share of the event:
{location_id or person_id, minutes?, percent?, remaining?} in place of
the id -- minutes (a fixed share), percent (of what the minutes leave),
and remaining true for the rest too. One given as a bare id takes the
remaining time, what the minutes and percents leave: each person all of
it, and the places an even part each. Each list's minutes must fit in
the event, and its percents add up to no more than 100. with_ids and
for_ids can name circles (get_circles) too, by id or as {circle_id,
except?, minutes?, percent?, remaining?}: a plain circle (kind
"circle") stands for its members now, each there (or it for each)
unless except names them, each taking its share whole, as a person
does; a community stands for itself, none of its members assumed, so
list those there too, and it takes no except. Notes and logs are for
the people there, a plain circle's members included; no one is both
with and for, through a circle or not.

judgments are how the event went for each person, judged after
compaction against each judgment part of the traits that apply to them
(see record_judgments): {person id: {trait id: {part key: {"rating",
"scale", "reasoning"}}}}. Set them to overwrite a rating by hand
(replacing them whole), or clear them.

repeat is write-only: given to create_event, or to update_event for an
event that isn't in a series, it makes the event the first of a
recurring series that repeats as it says (see Repeat), in the
calendar's time zone. The event's id becomes the series' own, and the
series' events (list_events) each get their own id, with the series'
as their recurring_event_id. It's never returned: get_recurrence says
how a series repeats, and update_recurrence changes it.

Everything before the last compaction (get_compaction_status's
last_compaction) is history: see update_event.

description_format.description:
How description is written: plain, html or markdown -- markdown
for what you write. None, it's HTML if it has tags, else plain

etag.description:
Which version of the event this is, as Calendar gives it; it
changes whenever the event does. Give it to update_event and delete_event -- the etag you last read: without it, the change is refused; changed since, the call is refused with every event that's changed, as it is now (_meta.conflicts) -- on a conflict, read it again: if what changed elsewhere is in fields you aren't changing, make your change again on it as it is now; if it's in fields you're changing, or it was deleted (or, deleting it, it was changed since), stop and ask the user -- showing what changed and what you meant to do -- and never overwrite their change, or put back what was deleted, without their OK.

every.description:
How often the series repeats: its events fall in every `interval`th
day, week, month or year.

interval.description:
1 for every day/week/month/year, 2 for every other one, and so on.
At least 1.

weekdays.description:
The days of the week events fall on, e.g. ["mon", "wed"]. Mostly
for `every` "week". With "day" it keeps only those days (every
weekday: "week" with all five is clearer); with "month" or "year"
it's every one of those weekdays in the month or year -- use
`nth_weekdays` for "the first Monday".

nth_weekdays.description:
Particular weekdays of the month, like the first Monday or the last
Friday. Only for `every` "month", or "year" with `months` set (each
then counts within those months). Can be given with `weekdays`.

month_days.description:
The days of the month events fall on: 1 to 31, or -1 for the last
day (months without a given day are skipped, so use -1 for "the end
of the month", not 31). Not for `every` "week".

months.description:
Only these months, 1 (January) to 12 (December). Mostly for `every`
"year", e.g. [11] with `nth_weekdays` for the 4th Thursday of
November.

count.description:
End the series after this many events, counting from its first.
Can't be given with `until`; give neither for a series that never
ends.

until.description:
End the series here: no event starts after it. A date ("2026-12-31")
means through the end of that day, in the series' time zone; a
datetime is exact. Can't be given with `count`.

week_starts_on.description:
The day weeks start on, which only matters for `every` "week" with
an `interval` above 1 and several `weekdays`: it decides which days
count as the same week. Monday when left out.

skipped.description:
Starts of events the series leaves out, e.g.
["2026-11-09T09:00:00-05:00"]. Each must be exactly the start the
rules give that event (a time without an offset is taken to be in the
series' time zone). (To cancel one event, cancelling it through
update_event is usually simpler.)

added.description:
Starts of extra events, beyond those the rules make, e.g.
["2026-12-01T14:00:00-05:00"] (a time without an offset is taken to
be in the series' time zone). Each lasts as long as the series'
events do.

description:
The judgments a compaction (by default the last one applied) calls
for, to make with record_judgments: each event with facts, with each
person it was about (the user, "self", and everyone there, for a
trait's "with" parts; everyone it was done for, for its "for" parts)
and the judgment parts of the traits that apply to them; then each of
those parts once -- its rubric and the ratings to choose from -- and
each person's history (what they did and where) over the days their
parts look back, their summaries of the trait facts those parts name
(`facts`), and each habit's note (`habit_notes`). Only those not made yet -- or with redo, all of
them, each event with the judgments already made (`current`), to
redo one with more context. Read-only.
name: prepare_judgments

instructions.default: JUDGE EACH ONE YOURSELF, without asking the user: they've already confirmed the facts, and the judgments are yours to make. `events` lists each event the compaction settled with facts, each person it was about, and the parts to judge for each of them ("<trait id>/<part key>"). Judge each event as the applied compaction's final timeline shows it -- its times, notes, actions and facts -- for that person alone, as it was for them. A part is in `parts` under "<trait id>/<part key>@<person id>" if there's one (that person's own), or else "<trait id>/<part key>": answer its rubric -- a "with" part for someone who was there, a "for" part for someone it was done for while they weren't -- from what the timeline, `facts` (each person's summaries of the trait facts its parts name -- "fact:<id>" -- as they are now, after the event) and `history` (what each person did and where over the days before) show, choosing one of its ratings (the number), with one succinct line of reasoning that names the fact it rests on. A habit of the user's ("habit:<id>") is judged like a person there, for how the event went as practice of that habit, its note in `habit_notes`. Where they don't say, rate what they do show rather than guess -- a judgment can be redone later. Record them all with record_judgments(compaction_id, judgments), each with request_id "<event id>/<person id>/<trait id>/<part key>"; the compaction isn't complete until every one is. Don't show the user the judgments unless they ask.

description:
A backfill of one habit's judgments (by id or name): for a habit
just made, or given a new rubric, whose settled events -- already
compacted -- aren't judged for it yet. Only when the user asks for
one: it's never part of a compaction. Gives a backfill_id, then, as
prepare_judgments does, each of its events in scope since `since`
(by default as far back as its judgment parts average over, and a
week of scores) until where history ends, with the parts to judge
for it; each part once; and its history. Only those not judged yet --
or with redo, all of them, each with the judgment already made
(`current`), to judge again. Make them yourself and record them with
record_judgments(backfill_id, judgments). Read-only.
name: prepare_habit_judgments

instructions.default: JUDGE EACH ONE YOURSELF, without asking the user: this is a backfill of one of their habits, the judgments of its settled events -- already compacted -- since `since`. `events` lists each, with the parts to judge for the habit ("<trait id>/<part key>"); `parts` gives each part's rubric and ratings once ("...@habit:<id>" for the habit's own), and `history` what the user did and where in its scope over the days before. Judge each event as it is on the calendar -- its times, notes, actions and facts -- for how it went as practice of the habit, its note in `habit_notes`, choosing one of the part's ratings (the number), with one succinct line of reasoning that names the fact it rests on. Record them all with record_judgments(backfill_id, judgments) -- the backfill_id where a compaction's id would go -- each with request_id "<event id>/habit:<id>/<trait id>/<part key>". With `current`, they're being redone: rate them afresh. Don't show the user the judgments unless they ask.

description:
Record judgments of a compaction's events (see prepare_judgments, and
the `judgments` an applied compaction returns) -- or, given a habit
backfill's backfill_id as compaction_id, of that habit's events (see
prepare_habit_judgments): each a request_id, a rating from that
request's ratings, and one succinct line of reasoning. Make them
yourself, never asking the user. They're kept on the events, by
person (or habit), trait and part; a judgment recorded again replaces
the earlier one. Returns how many were recorded, the ids of any
requests still to judge, and whether that completes the compaction
(or the backfill).

Judgment.description:
A judgment made: the request's id, a rating from its ratings, and
one succinct line of reasoning.

description:
When the user's scheduled routines usually run -- the ones that
compact notes into a proposal, and answer the notes left on it: each
a time of day ("07:30", 24-hour, in the calendar's time_zone, given
too) with an optional label ("Morning compaction"), earliest first.

description:
Say when the user's scheduled routines run, replacing the hints
whole: each a time of day ("HH:MM", 24-hour, in the calendar's time
zone -- see get_compaction_schedule_hints) and an optional label
("Morning compaction"). A scheduled routine that compacts notes into a
proposal, or answers the notes left on one, should keep these up to
date, its own time among them, so the user's app fetches what it made
soon after it runs; the app can't change them. Keep the other hints
there: get them first, and send them back with yours. Times are
unique; an empty list clears them. Returns them as saved.
